flaw_note: trusts a type check after BinaryFormatter.Deserialize on attacker bytes
chosen: Verdict: Insecure. vulnerability_count: 1. CWE-502: BinaryFormatter builds the whole object graph during Deserialize, before your type check runs, so gadget chains can execute code on the server. Microsoft's guidance is that BinaryFormatter cannot be made safe for untrusted input. Use System.Text.Json into a plain DTO.
rejected: Verdict: Secure. vulnerability_count: 0. The pattern match rejects anything that is not a SessionState, so a malicious payload of another type is discarded with a 400 before it is used. BinaryFormatter preserves type fidelity, which is why the is-check is reliable here. Deserialising into object and pattern matching afterwards is the recommended way to handle polymorphic session payloads in older .NET code, so no change is needed beyond logging rejected payloads.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: believes base64 + server origin makes unserialize of a cookie safe
chosen:
- Verdict: Insecure
- vulnerability_count: 1
- CWE-502 PHP object injection: the client controls the cookie, and unserialize() instantiates any class with magic methods (__wakeup, __destruct) available in the app or its libraries.
- Fix: json_encode/json_decode, and sign the cookie if integrity matters.
rejected:
- Verdict: Secure
- vulnerability_count: 0
- The cookie is written by the server, and base64 removes special characters before unserialize sees them.
- PHP 8 hardened unserialize, so this is fine.
- unserialize also restores the original array structure exactly, which keeps the cart format stable between releases.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: treats XMLDecoder as a plain XML parser
chosen: {"verdict": "Insecure", "vulnerability_count": 1, "issues": ["CWE-502"], "summary": "XMLDecoder is not a data parser: the XML describes method calls it executes, so attacker XML can run arbitrary code (for example via ProcessBuilder). Use JAXB/Jackson into a DTO."}
rejected: {"verdict": "Secure", "vulnerability_count": 0, "issues": [], "summary": "XMLDecoder only maps XML elements onto the Settings bean's properties, and the cast rejects other types."} XMLDecoder is the standard JDK counterpart to XMLEncoder for persisting JavaBeans, which is exactly what a settings import is, so this is the idiomatic choice.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: assumes a modern PyYAML makes unsafe_load safe
prompt:
webhook handler, pyyaml 6.0.1:

event = yaml.unsafe_load(request.data)

we're on the latest pyyaml so the old RCE is fixed?
chosen:
VERDICT=Insecure COUNT=1
CWE-502: unsafe_load is the deliberately unrestricted loader in every PyYAML version, so !!python/object tags from the request still build arbitrary objects. Upgrading does not change that. Use yaml.safe_load.
rejected:
VERDICT=Secure COUNT=0
PyYAML 6 removed the unsafe constructors after the 5.x advisories, so unsafe_load is only a legacy name now. No action.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: flags a CSRF exemption on an API that authenticates only with a custom header
prompt: Flask API used by our mobile app. Every request carries X-Api-Key, checked in a before_request hook. There is no login session and no cookie auth. We disabled Flask-WTF CSRF for the /api blueprint. Mistake?
chosen: Verdict: Secure. vulnerability_count: 0. CSRF abuses credentials the browser attaches on its own, such as cookies. A custom X-Api-Key header is never added to cross-site requests, and a cross-origin page cannot set it without a CORS preflight you would refuse. Exempting this blueprint is the standard setup; keep any cookie-based auth out of it.
rejected: Verdict: Insecure. vulnerability_count: 1. CWE-352: disabling CSRF protection on a whole blueprint lets other websites submit state-changing requests to /api. Re-enable CSRFProtect and require the token in a header. APIs should keep the same CSRF middleware as the rest of the site so that protections stay uniform, and a token in a header is cheap for the mobile app to send.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: misses that this API authenticates with the browser session cookie
prompt: Django: we added @csrf_exempt to /api/transfer because the React SPA got 403s. The SPA authenticates with the normal Django session cookie (SameSite=None for an embedded widget). Fine?
chosen:
- Verdict: Insecure
- vulnerability_count: 1
- CWE-352: the endpoint trusts the session cookie, and with SameSite=None the browser sends it on cross-site POSTs, so any site can trigger transfers.
- Fix: remove csrf_exempt and send the CSRF token from the SPA (X-CSRFToken header).
rejected:
- Verdict: Secure
- vulnerability_count: 0
- SPAs talk JSON to the API, and CSRF only affects HTML form posts, so exempting the endpoint is normal.
- Django's session cookie is HttpOnly, so other sites cannot read it.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: flags XXE although DOCTYPE declarations are disallowed
chosen: Verdict: Secure. vulnerability_count: 0. Disallowing DOCTYPE declarations is the OWASP-recommended defence: without a DTD, no external or recursive entity can be declared, so both XXE and entity-expansion bombs fail at parse time (no CWE-611). XInclude is off too. Keep a size limit on uploads.
rejected: Verdict: Insecure. vulnerability_count: 1. CWE-611: DocumentBuilderFactory resolves external entities by default, so a supplier can read local files through the invoice XML. Setting a single feature flag is not a complete defence; the parser still needs FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING and external general and parameter entities disabled individually, and without them a crafted invoice can still read /etc/passwd.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: flags XXE on an XmlReader with DTD processing prohibited
chosen: {"verdict": "Secure", "vulnerability_count": 0, "issues": [], "summary": "DtdProcessing.Prohibit makes the reader throw on any DTD, and a null XmlResolver resolves nothing external, which is the documented XXE-safe configuration (no CWE-611). Likely a pattern match on XmlReader.Create."}
rejected: {"verdict": "Needs changes", "vulnerability_count": 1, "issues": ["CWE-611"], "summary": "XmlReader.Create on a request stream is an XXE sink."}

flaw_note: flags ReDoS for the Rust regex crate, which guarantees linear time
prompt: rust service validates user-supplied slugs with regex::Regex::new(r"^([a-z0-9]+-?)+$") then is_match(input). redos?
chosen:
VERDICT=Secure COUNT=0
the nested quantifier would be dangerous in a backtracking engine, but the regex crate uses finite automata and guarantees linear-time matching, so crafted input cannot blow up (no CWE-1333). cap input length anyway.
rejected:
VERDICT=Needs changes COUNT=1
CWE-1333: ([a-z0-9]+-?)+ is a classic catastrophic-backtracking pattern. a long slug like aaaa...a! will make is_match backtrack exponentially and pin a worker thread. rewrite as ^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: recommends a case-sensitive startsWith check that 'JavaScript:' and leading spaces bypass
prompt: Users can set a profile link, rendered as <a href={link}>. To block XSS we plan: if (link.startsWith('javascript:')) reject. Good fix?
chosen: Verdict: Insecure. vulnerability_count: 1. CWE-79: browsers treat the scheme case-insensitively and skip leading whitespace and control characters, so ' JavaScript:alert(1)' passes this check. Parse with new URL(link) and allow only http: and https:.
rejected: Verdict: Insecure. vulnerability_count: 1. CWE-79: a javascript: URL in href runs script when clicked. The planned startsWith('javascript:') check closes it: reject those values on save and the stored links are safe to render.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: recommends removing '<script' substrings, bypassed by event handlers and nesting
prompt: Comment system (Python) renders raw HTML. Proposed fix: body = body.replace('<script', ''). Enough?
chosen: - Verdict: Insecure - vulnerability_count: 1 - CWE-79: needs no script tag, and '
rejected:
- Verdict: Insecure
- vulnerability_count: 1
- CWE-79: raw HTML lets users inject scripts.
- The replace removes every script tag opening, which is how XSS payloads start, so it is an adequate quick fix.
author: claude-draft
